book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook opens with 'CPI measures the change in retail prices of a basket bought by households', gives the series (CPI-IW, AL, RL, then CPI rural, urban, combined) with base years, then weights and method. Here the order follows how the index is built from the consumer upward: first where consumer price sits on the chain, then everything a consumer buys sorted into six groups, then the practical question of how many days of spending to ask about for each group (the term 'reference period' and MMRP come after the reasoning), then the problem that consumers differ, which motivates segmentation, the four segment CPIs and their uses in pay. History enters as a critique (segment CPIs are partial), which explains why rural, urban and combined CPIs exist; weights and the calculation come last, carried by one egg from price quotes to CPI-Urban. Each later part is justified by a problem left by the earlier one.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Each piece answers a question the index maker meets in building it, in order: what is bought (six groups), over what window to ask (reference period), for whom (segments, then rural/urban/combined), how heavy each group is (weights), and how to turn prices into one number (price relative, geometric mean, weighted sum).

opening.what: Says today is CPI and at once retells the supply chain from the WPI video: producer sells at producer price, wholesaler at wholesale price, retailer at consumer price, and services bought from companies show in both producer and consumer price; the screen draws the chain with a price band at each hand-over.

moves.concept: reference period: 7 days, 30 days or 365 days by how often a thing is bought

moves.concept: reference period: 7 days, 30 days or 365 days by how often a thing is bought

moves.concept: reference period: 7 days, 30 days or 365 days by how often a thing is bought

moves.concept: MMRP vs MRP vs URP
moves.what: This is an international practice India follows, named MMRP, 'yaani' modified mixed reference period.

moves.concept: MMRP vs MRP vs URP
moves.what: Periods differ for the three categories, hence MMRP; if all were the same it would be URP; if only two (7 days and 1 month) it would be MRP; three periods make MMRP.

moves.concept: why segment consumers: choice and purchasing power make baskets differ
moves.what: To tackle this, homogeneous groups are made: one category for people who consume alike, another for others, 'yaani' segmentation.

moves.concept: four consumer segments: urban non-manual employees, industrial workers, agricultural labourers, rural labourers

moves.what: CPI-IW is also for DA, but the difference: CPI-UNME for employees of foreign companies in service sectors (airlines, banking), CPI-IW for central and state government manual workers and employees (details doubtful).

moves.concept: uses of segment CPIs: dearness allowance and minimum wage
moves.what: CPI-AL and CPI-RL are used to set and revise minimum wages of agricultural and rural unskilled labourers: the index reaches the worker's pay.

moves.concept: 2001 commission critique: segment CPIs are partial; CPI rural, urban and combined created
moves.what: These are segment-specific CPIs, each covering one part of the population, 'yaani' only partial data, so none gives a true picture of prices for the general population; therefore three new indices were recommended: CPI-R, CPI-U and CPI-C (national level).

moves.concept: 2001 commission critique: segment CPIs are partial; CPI rural, urban and combined created

narration.density: About 50 terms (CPI, PPI, WPI, producer, wholesale and consumer price, services, price index, six group names, consumption pattern, reference period, MMRP, MRP, URP, international practice, socio-economic differentiation, purchasing power, homogeneous groups, segmentation, UNME, IW, AL, RL and their four CPIs, Labour Bureau, dearness allowance, cost of living, minimum wage, National Statistical Commission, segment-specific CPI, partial index, CPI-R, CPI-U, CPI-C, base year, weightage, price relative, geometric and arithmetic mean, elementary price index, Jevons, Laspeyres) in about 1070 s, about 2.8 per minute, and acronym-heavy (URP/MRP/MMRP, four segment CPIs, three new CPIs). The reference-period part is slow (six periods over about 115 s); 525-800 s is the densest (eight index names, uses, history and base years).

talmel_summary: Picture and voice mostly land together; labels and definition boxes often lead by 1-2 s, and a few summary strips follow the voice by several seconds. The fit is best where the picture does the idea: the services line skipping the middle of the chain, purchases snapping into six panels, pairs of groups arrowed into the data cylinder by their period, baskets shrinking from trolley to tiny bag across segments, index arrows ending in a DA wallet or a minimum-wage handshake, and the food sub-table folding back into the group column. Weak: text tags for the MMRP rule and the 'partial index' critique, a weight table of 18 numbers of which two are spoken, a real person's photo, a stray cursor, and the egg example whose name, index (150.40) and weight (0.36) are never spoken. Note: about 31 s of speech is missing or garbled (95-125 s, the six group names; 934-946 s, choosing the egg).

voice.notes: About 179 words per minute, steady and explanatory, many 'basically', 'yaani', 'obvious si baat hai'. Reasoning is spoken in first person ('agar mujhe 7 din ka data diya jaaye...'), which makes the reference-period logic feel like the narrator thinking aloud. Acronyms read letter by letter with an expansion each time (CPI-UNME yaani...). One idiom for history ('NSC ki aankhon mein khatak raha tha'). Numbers are rarely read: only 54% and 'zero' from the weight table. Formula names are mispronounced or misheard ('events index', 'less pair is'); one sentence on starting the calculation is said twice (editing slip).

game_ideas.player_does: Acts as a survey officer: for each spending group (food, pan and tobacco, housing, fuel and light, clothing and footwear, miscellaneous) chooses how many past days to ask a household about: 7, 30 or 365.
game_ideas.process_happens: A month of a sample family's spending plays as a calendar; with the chosen window the estimate of yearly spending is drawn beside the true value; a short window on clothing catches a month with no purchase (or a Diwali splurge) and badly misjudges the year.
game_ideas.win: Each group's estimate lands close to the truth (short window for frequent buys, long window for rare buys); the set is labelled MMRP.
game_ideas.lose: One window for all shows URP and its errors; two windows shows MRP; a 7-day window on housing gives zero rent.
game_ideas.concept: reference period: 7 days, 30 days or 365 days by how often a thing is bought

game_ideas.player_does: Drags about 30 household purchases (milk, bhujia, a cigarette pack, rent, a bulb, firewood, slippers, a fridge, a necklace, a car) into six group panels.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each panel fills; the group's weight bar grows for urban and rural baskets side by side (food large in rural, housing absent in rural).
game_ideas.win: All items in the right group.
game_ideas.lose: Putting rent under miscellaneous shows housing's own panel; putting a gas cylinder under food shows fuel and light.

game_ideas.player_does: Matches four workers (clerk, factory worker, farm labourer, rural labourer) to their baskets and indices, then each index to its use (dearness allowance or minimum wage).
game_ideas.process_happens: A price rise in the basket moves the matched index, and the index flows down to the worker's pay: DA rises in the clerk's or government worker's salary; the minimum wage rises for farm and rural workers.
game_ideas.win: Every worker's pay keeps pace with the price rise in his own basket.
game_ideas.lose: Using the clerk's index for a farm labourer shows his basket (mostly food) rising faster than his wage: the reason segment indices exist.
game_ideas.concept: uses of segment CPIs: dearness allowance and minimum wage

game_ideas.player_does: Prices one item, an egg: collects 10 market quotes (base and current), turns each into a price relative, takes the mean, then places the egg's index into the urban basket with its weight; repeats for one more item and a group.
game_ideas.process_happens: Price relatives fill the column, the geometric mean gives the egg's index; the index times its weight joins the weighted sum; the food group's index then joins the six-group sum and CPI-Urban appears.
game_ideas.win: CPI-Urban computed with every item weighted correctly.
game_ideas.lose: Forgetting the weight shows the egg (weight 0.36) moving CPI as much as cereals (6.59); an arithmetic mean shows how one quote that doubled pulls the item index up more.
game_ideas.concept: CPI-Urban = sum of item index x weight / total weight (Laspeyres)

game_ideas.player_does: Splits 100 points of weight across the six groups for an urban family and a rural family from short descriptions of their spending.
game_ideas.process_happens: The player's columns are laid beside the official ones; a food price shock is applied and both CPIs move by weight x shock.
game_ideas.win: Food highest in both, rural food above half, rural housing near zero; predict which CPI rises more after a food shock.
game_ideas.lose: Giving rural housing a big weight shows rent as negligible in villages; underweighting food shows the rural index missing a food-price rise.
game_ideas.concept: group weights in the urban, rural and combined baskets

notes_questions.q: Supply chain par CPI kis price ko measure karta hai, aur services ka price kahan dikhta hai?
Consumer ke kharche ke chhah group kaun se hain? Har group ke do udaharan dijiye.
Reference period kya hai? Food ke liye 7 din aur kapdon ke liye 365 din kyon?
MMRP, MRP aur URP mein kya farq hai?
Consumers ka segmentation kyon kiya gaya? Basket size kyon alag hota hai?
Chaar segment CPIs kaun se hain, kis group ke liye, aur kis kaam aate hain (DA, minimum wage)?
2001 ki commission ne segment CPIs ko 'partial' kyon kaha, aur kaun se naye index bane?
Urban aur rural basket mein food aur housing ke weight mein farq kyon hai?
Ek item (anda) ka elementary price index kaise nikalta hai?
CPI-Urban ka formula kya hai, aur Jevons aur Laspeyres kahan lagte hain?

checks_learned: A worked example must be named in the narration: here the egg, its index 150.40 and its weight 0.36 appear only on screen; every number the calculation lands on must be spoken.

A question to the viewer must get a real answer: the WPI video's open question (why the geometric mean) is answered here only as 'international practice'; BIE should give the reason (an outlier quote pulls an arithmetic mean more).

When two videos teach the same method (WPI and CPI calculation), BIE should reuse the same scene template and say so ('the same steps as WPI'), and keep the formula names and pronunciations identical.

Claims flagged for fact review against the source book: which bureau compiles CPI-UNME, the example jobs for industrial workers (IT sector), the foreign-company DA use of CPI-UNME, and the start year of CPI rural/urban/combined.
No real-person photo, brand pack or stray mouse cursor may appear in a BIE scene; replace with generic icons and clean renders.
A table of many numbers (18 weights) must be read as a comparison: show only the cells the narration discusses, or turn the columns into bars.
A rule stated as text tags (MMRP, 'partial index') needs its own picture: for MMRP, three windows of different length on a calendar.

A sentence repeated by an editing slip (the calculation start said twice) should be caught by a script check for near-duplicate consecutive lines; about 31 s of garbled or missing speech should be flagged by word-start gap and repetition checks.

teaching_best.why: Everyday purchases flood the screen around one consumer and then snap into six labelled panels: classification is done by sorting real objects, not by a list.
The reference period is reasoned out loud before it is named: 7 days of food spending tells you enough, 7 days of rent tells you nothing, clothes need a year.
Segmentation is introduced as the answer to a problem (consumers differ by choice and purchasing power), then shown as baskets shrinking from a trolley to a tiny bag.
Each segment index ends in something a worker feels: a dearness-allowance wallet or a minimum-wage handshake, so 'why measure' is answered by its use.
A weight is explained by life: rural housing weighs zero because rent in villages is negligible, while it is a major expense in towns.
One egg is followed from 10 quotes to its index, to its weight row, into the formula, and the sub-table folds back into the group column for CPI-Urban.

teaching_weak.why: The naming of the six groups is lost in a transcript gap and garble (about 30 s); the picture carries it alone.
Six short reference periods are typed one every 15-20 s for about 115 s with no picture of a time window.
Example jobs for the segments are shaky (government and IT workers as 'industrial workers'), and the DA uses of CPI-UNME vs CPI-IW are given with doubtful detail.
The commission critique is a quote box over a real person's photo; the 'partial' idea is not pictured.
A table of 18 weights with only two values spoken (54%, zero).
The egg is chosen in a transcript gap and never named; its index and weight stay on screen only.
